extracted.intended_audience: artists, art students, critics, and educated readers interested in art theory and the practice of landscape painting
extracted.subtask_description: Theoretical/practical criteria for evaluating and producing landscape painting, especially the qualities of 'execution' (mechanical handling) and the primacy of truth in art. Covers what makes execution powerful or vicious, the two ends of landscape art (facts vs. thoughts), and how perception and training affect judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of execution
rubrics_metrics.description: By the term "execution," I understand the right mechanical use of the means of art to produce a given end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Execution is the correct, mechanical employment of artistic means toward an intended result. It is a practical, instrumental standard: are the tools and techniques used appropriately to achieve the artist's end?

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth (first quality of execution)
rubrics_metrics.description: The first quality of execution is truth. All qualities of execution ... are influenced by, and in a great degree dependent on, a far higher power than that of mere execution,--knowledge of truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Truth: delicate, ceaseless expression of refined truth carried to the last touch; precision of the instantaneous line is the source of difference between commonplace and perfect work. If truth is present, other qualities may be spared. Anti-pattern: swift or showy handling that sacrifices truth is a fatal vice ('what was once imperfection, is now falsehood').

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity (second quality of execution)
rubrics_metrics.description: The second quality of execution is simplicity. The more unpretending, quiet, and retiring the means, the more impressive their effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid ostentation, brilliancy, or rendering lines attractive at the expense of meaning. Simplicity withdraws attention from means to result. Exhibition of technique for its own sake is vice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mystery (third quality of execution)
rubrics_metrics.description: The third is mystery. Nature is always mysterious and secret in the use of her means; and art is always likest her when it is most inexplicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The best execution is that which is incomprehensible and defies imitation (other qualities being equal). Mystery causes the spectator to attend to the result rather than the means.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inadequacy (fourth quality of execution)
rubrics_metrics.description: The fourth is inadequacy. The less sufficient the means appear to the end, the greater ... will be the sensation of power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An appearance that the means are insufficient can heighten the sensation of power in the result. This is a strategic, paradoxical device: apparent insufficiency amplifies the perceived accomplishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision (fifth quality of execution)
rubrics_metrics.description: The fifth is decision: the appearance, that is, that whatever is done, has been done fearlessly and at once; because this gives us the impression that both the fact to be represented, and the means necessary to its representation, were perfectly known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decision produces the impression of confidence and knowledge. It is the visible conviction that the artist knew the subject and how to render it. Anti-pattern: decision without foundation (boldness lacking truth) is a vice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Velocity (sixth quality of execution)
rubrics_metrics.description: The sixth is velocity. ... of two touches, as nearly as possible the same in other respects, the quickest will invariably be the best.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quick, decisive touches tend to have more evenness, grace, variety, and natural qualities (gradation, uncertainty, unity). Velocity is attractive but must be subordinate to truth and simplicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strangeness (illegitimate seventh source of pleasure in execution)
rubrics_metrics.description: I might have added a seventh--strangeness, which in many cases is productive of a pleasure ... Though it adds to our impression if the means used be such as we should never have thought of, ... yet strangeness is not to be considered as a legitimate source of pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strangeness can delight but is illegitimate because it relies on the spectator's ignorance. The means most conducive to the end should be most pleasurable; when strangeness pleases, it often indicates a lack of understanding in the viewer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance among execution qualities; beware sacrificing higher to lower
rubrics_metrics.description: These six qualities are the only perfectly legitimate sources of pleasure in execution ... some are so far inconsistent with others, that they cannot be united in high degrees ... the danger of too great fondness for those sensations of power which are associated with the three last qualities ... the moment the higher qualities are sacrificed to them ... we have a brilliant vice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize tensions: mystery/simplicity (withdraw attention from means) versus inadequacy/decision/velocity (draw attention to means). Do not sacrifice truth and simplicity to achieve showy decision or speed. Examples: Berghem and Salvator Rosa as cases where fondness for power produced vicious execution; unnamed modern artist who lost truth and beauty to swiftness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illegitimate 'noble vices' and contemptible technical vices
rubrics_metrics.description: There are, on the other hand, qualities of execution which are often sought for and praised ... and these are vice throughout ... Such is that which is often thought so desirable ... under the title of boldness ... such, on the other hand, the softness and smoothness ... and such the exhibition of particular powers and tricks of the hand ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warnings against common technical vices: exaggerated broadness of touch, excessive softness/smoothness (Carlo Dolci), trivial 'tricks' and exhibitions of manual skill that forget any artistic end. These are outright vices with no redeeming aim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sublimity defined as elevation of mind
rubrics_metrics.description: Sublimity is the effect upon the mind of anything above it ... anything which elevates the mind is sublime ... Greatness of matter, space, power, virtue, or beauty, are thus all sublime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sublimity is not a separate class of ideas but a mode of effect produced by greatness. For art, aim for works that elevate the mind through greatness of subject or conception. Note: it's the contemplation of greatness (defiance, calm prophecy), not the immediate shudder of terror, that is sublime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two great ends of landscape painting: representation of facts
rubrics_metrics.description: The two great ends of landscape painting are the representation of facts and thoughts. ... The first, to induce in the spectator's mind the faithful conception of any natural objects whatsoever ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First end: place the spectator before the landscape, enabling independent perception of facts. This requires fidelity to observable nature; it is a necessary foundation for higher aims and can be judged by attention to factual representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two great ends of landscape painting: representation of thoughts
rubrics_metrics.description: The second, to guide the spectator's mind to those objects most worthy of its contemplation, and to inform him of the thoughts and feelings with which these were regarded by the artist himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Second end: the artist acts as companion and teacher, sharing feelings and directing thought. This is the higher aim of art—conveying an individual mind's conception. It presupposes and requires the first end (truth in facts) as foundation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of material depends on the artist's aim
rubrics_metrics.description: Each of these different aims of art will necessitate a different system of choice of objects to be represented. ... The first does not indeed imply choice at all ... the artist aiming at the second end, selects his objects for their meaning and character, rather than for their beauty ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If your aim is faithful representation, choose persistently pleasing natural objects; if your aim is to convey thought, choose subjects for their meaning. Selection should serve the intended end rather than be driven by convention or mere technical rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of sameness and repetition from the first mode
rubrics_metrics.description: The first mode of selection apt to produce sameness and repetition. ... It tends to induce constant repetition of the same ideas, and reference to the same principles; it gives rise to those 'rules' of art ... which are the curse of art and the crown of the connoisseur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware that purely factual, rule-bound selection can degenerate into formulaic work. Cultivate reflection to avoid mere technical repetition and to reach the pure ideal where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of truth: nothing atones for falsehood
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing can atone for the want of truth, not the most brilliant imagination ... not the most exalted conception ... All falsehood must be a blot as well as a sin, an injury as well as a deception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat truth (accurate knowledge of nature/facts) as the indispensable foundation for all art. False foundations render higher imagination corrupt; avoid inventing or distorting facts to serve imaginative ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth is a practical criterion for judging artists
rubrics_metrics.description: It is in the power of all, with care and time, to form something like a just judgment ... with respect to the representation of facts, it is possible for all, by attention, to form a right judgment ... Truth is a bar of comparison ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For critical judgments accessible to many viewers, use fidelity to truth (representation of facts) as the test. While appreciation of imaginative content may be restricted to sympathetic minds, truthfulness in depiction can be fairly assessed by attentive viewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception of truth requires cultivation; uneducated senses mislead
rubrics_metrics.description: That the truth of nature is not to be discerned by the uneducated senses. ... until this cultivation has been bestowed ... it is as absurd as it is audacious to pretend to form any judgment whatsoever respecting the truth of art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume native vision suffices. Training in observation, practice in scrutinizing form, shade, and color, and cultivation of judgment are necessary before one can judge fidelity to nature. Critics and viewers must be educated to perceive truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attention, reflection, and memory are necessary for sight
rubrics_metrics.description: The first great mistake ... is the supposition that they must 'see' a thing if it be before their eyes. ... unless the minds of men are particularly directed to the impressions of sight, objects pass perpetually before the eyes without conveying any impression to the brain at all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perceptual seeing requires active attention. Encourage practices that train attention and use reflection and memory to retain and recognize visual facts; mere passive seeing is inadequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensibility and moral feeling sharpen perception
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree of ignorance ... depends ... partly on a natural want of sensibility to the power of beauty of form ... With this kind of bodily sensibility ... is intimately connected that higher sensibility which we revere as one of the chief attributes of all noble minds ... perception is so quickened by love, and judgment so tempered by veneration ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate sensibility—both physical acuity for color/form and the moral/emotional temperament (love, veneration)—to enhance perception of truth. Without this, perceptual faculties may remain blunt despite intellectual effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sight depends on previous knowledge; imagination can mislead ('we see what we know')
rubrics_metrics.description: How sight depends upon previous knowledge. ... The more sensibility and imagination a man possesses, the more likely will he be to fall into error; for then he will see whatever he expects, and admire and judge with his heart, and not with his eyes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of confirmation bias in visual perception: prior beliefs, cultural expectations, and imagination can cause viewers to 'see' what they know rather than what is. Training should include learning to separate expectation from observed fact. Examples: misconceptions about Italian skies' blueness; children drawing perspectives; non-European viewers misunderstanding perspective or shade.
